title: PixiJS scenes, written as JSX.
headings: Signals drive the scene Cleanup is automatic Testable headless Code example
text: SolidJS 2 · PixiJS 8 pixi-solid renders every major PixiJS display object as a component, so your scene graph is reactive, typed, and testable without a browser. Props bind to Pixi objects, one effect per key, so an update touches one property. Components destroy the instances they own and detach the ones they do not. Context, hooks and ticker run without a GPU, so scenes mount in jsdom.

title: 2D Content on a 3D Surface
headings: Building a texture Options Reactivity Rendering only when it changes Orientation Cleanup
text: A 3D material can sample any texture, including one showing live 2D content. Use it for in-world screens, signs, labels, scoreboards, or UI panels attached to a model. ships for this, but using it directly has three sharp edges. Pose the renderer, remember that its runs on rather than the ticker your app runs, and free the render target yourself. handles all three. A live 2D panel on a 3D surface. The uptime and draw-call lines update every frame: The hook takes pixi-solid JSX and returns a texture. The JSX arrives already filled with its children, because the parent component binds them: The hook must run inside a or , because it reads the renderer and the ticker from context. It throws a clear error if neither is present. Two constraints come from itself: It draws one container, so wrap several roots in a . The container is built once. Structure inside it ( , ) stays reactive; replacing the whole tree needs a new texture. You do not call . Content updates are drawn on the next frame, because defaults to . The content is mounted once, like any JSX tree, so internal structure stays reactive while the top-level tree does not rebuild: changing updates the text, and the next frame draws it. Swapping the entire tree needs a new texture. Re-rendering costs one pass over the content every frame. For a texture that changes once a minute, such as a clock or a scoreboard nobody is looking at, turn the loop off and render on demand: skips the initial run, since the texture was drawn when it was built. This is an optimisation, not the normal path: leave on until a profile suggests otherwise. The image is stored the other way up from an image texture. It shows upright on a default or the sides of a , and upside down where an image would be upright: a , a plane with , a loaded model, or a 2D . On those, flip the object that shows it: The hook destroys the render target when its component unmounts, and leaves your content alone, since those components clean up after themselves. If you need the texture to outlive the component, use directly and drive it yourself.

After swapping a material on a slot, call . For a value that differs per slot, such as a tint or a fade, declare and write it. A field can hold up to four numbers per slot: To rewrite many slots in one pass, write into and call . binds the same 3D transform and event props as every other scene node, so , and work as usual. title: Meshes and Materials
headings: 1. Declarative Nested Components (Automatic Disposal) Changing size, and changing shape Conditional Swapping with <Show> or <Switch> 2. Instantiated Object Props (Resource Sharing) Summary of Lifecycles Available Declarative Geometries Available Declarative Materials
text: provides to render 3D geometry combined with materials. Four geometries and all four material types, on a turntable: In 3D rendering engines like PixiJS 3D, GPU resources (buffers, textures, and shader pipeline descriptors) are expensive to allocate. gives you two ways to work with geometries and materials: Declarative Nested Components (Recommended for component-scoped resources) : Material options stay live, and the resource is disposed automatically on unmount. Instantiated Object Props (Recommended for shared / global resources) : Pass pre-created class instances where you retain ownership and manage lifecycle. When geometries and materials are placed as direct JSX children of , manages their lifecycle for you. When the component unmounts or conditionally swaps, it calls automatically. Furthermore, updating properties like , , or updates the existing GPU material directly with zero allocations. A geometry's options are read when it is built — turns them into vertex buffers and keeps no settable copy — so changing a geometry option after mount does not reshape it. Materials are the opposite: their options are live fields, so follows the signal. To make something bigger, scale the mesh . That is a transform, so it costs nothing and updates every frame: To change the shape itself — segments, radius, a different geometry altogether — mount a new geometry. Inside , remounts it and disposes the old one: Scaling is not always equivalent: anything that reads vertex positions, such as the dissolve bit's holes, works in the geometry's stored units and therefore scales with the mesh. Those need a rebuilt geometry, which is why the two are separate operations. You can conditionally swap materials or geometries using standard SolidJS primitives. When the condition flips, the old material is automatically destroyed, and the new one takes its place: If you have a geometry or material that is shared across hundreds of meshes (e.g., enemy particles, terrain tiles, or trees in a forest), you should create a single instance outside the component tree and pass it as a prop. When passed as a prop, treats it as user-owned and will never destroy it when an individual mesh unmounts: — lies in XY with a +Z normal, so a quarter turn on X makes it a floor — PBR metallic-roughness material. — Unlit flat color or texture. — Classic Blinn-Phong material. — Cel-shaded stylized toon material.

title: Portals and Render Textures
headings: Showing a render texture A real portal Disposing
text: shows a render texture on a surface. That covers two jobs: A window onto another view — a security monitor, a picture frame, a teleporter face. You supply a render texture from anywhere, such as a second camera. A real portal — a doorway that leads somewhere else in the same scene. This needs the pass below as well. The render texture is always yours: you create it, size it, and destroy it. is a shortcut for the material's slot, and tints it. Leave out and the surface shows plain until you assign . is written as a child of , so it is created, updated and destroyed with the mesh. See Meshes and Materials for the ownership rules the other materials follow. A portal is two quads facing their local : entry — the surface the viewer looks through, drawn with . exit — the quad on the far side. The room the portal shows sits in front of it. Each frame, puts a camera behind the exit where the viewer is in front of the entry, renders the scene through it into the feed, and the entry shows the result. Because the entry shows that image at the viewer's own screen position, it reads as an opening rather than a picture. The meshes are built as instances because the pass needs them at construction. adopts them, so the components add them to the view and leave destroying them to you. Note the two imports: is 's class, while is the component. Three rules decide whether it looks right: Size the feed to the view, and resize it with the view. Another aspect ratio stretches the far side, and too few pixels blur it. Give both quads the same . A scale only one of them has carries into the portal camera and distorts the far side. Use a perspective camera and an unrotated view. With an orthographic camera the far side does not show, and in a rotated view the image does not line up with the opening. runs at the stage, so its position in does not matter; it always finishes before the scene draws the entry. frees its own resources when the view is destroyed. title: Post Effects and Passes
headings: Adding passes Toggling and tuning Available passes Render to texture Why there is no <Bloom> component
text: A pass runs after the 3D scene draws. It can tint the whole image, add bloom, or copy an output such as normals into a texture you keep. Passes belong to the view , not to a node, because they change everything the view draws. Bloom and an outline pass on emissive materials. Drag to orbit: Build the pass with and hand it to the view through . The order of the array is the order they run in. With the view owns the passes, so they go on the provider with the other viewport options: Construct passes once, outside the component if nothing reactive feeds them. The array is copied when you assign it, so a new array literal each render re-initialises the graph. Turn a pass on and off with . This leaves the render graph alone, so it is cheap enough for a settings toggle: Options that have setters can be driven the same way, from a signal: Do not toggle by rebuilding the array. Reassigning it invalidates the graph, while costs nothing. and on , and anything else the class exposes as read-only, are constructor options. Change those by rebuilding the pass. For an effect of your own, extend (or ) from and add the instance to . copies a scene output — colour, normals or velocity — into a texture your app keeps. Use it when the result has to leave the view, for example to show it on a 2D sprite, or to feed a compositor of your own. An effect that reads an output within the same frame, such as an upscaler, should read it in its own pass rather than through , so it is not copied out first. Every other 3D node has a component, so the absence here is deliberate. A pass is view-wide. A component that registered itself from wherever it was mounted could change the rendering of content it knows nothing about. Passes are therefore declared only where the view is declared: the prop. is already declarative. Order is the array order, and the set of passes is a plain list you can read. A component per effect would add nothing. It would shadow upstream class names, repeat their option types, and drift every time adds a pass. Effects are constructed once and tuned through setters, which JSX props do not improve on. Reactivity has a better answer. toggles a pass without touching the graph, whereas a JSX would reassign and rebuild it. If JSX ordering is ever worth having, it can be added as one thin component — — that registers into the enclosing view and does nothing else. That would sit beside , not replace it.

title: Loading an Asset Manifest
headings: What is an Asset Manifest? Example assets-manifest.json Example: Loading Assets from a Manifest Further reading
text: For applications with many assets, managing individual asset loading can become cumbersome. PixiJS provides an Asset Manifest system that lets you define all your assets, their paths, and groups in a single JSON file. Use PixiJS AssetPack to generate the manifest for you. This guide demonstrates how to load an entire asset manifest and then access the loaded assets within your application. An asset manifest is a JSON file that describes your application's assets. It typically includes: : Groups of assets that can be loaded together. This is extremely useful for loading assets required for a specific scene or component. : Individual assets with their unique (how you refer to them in code) and (their file path). Let's assume you have an file in your folder like this: Loading a manifest resolves to , so the memo reports when the bundles are ready rather than returning the assets. Components then read each asset by its alias as they need it. The boundary renders its while the bundles load, so the page can show a DOM loading indicator before any Pixi object exists. When a scene needs only a few known assets, return them from the memo and read them directly instead. See loading individual assets . Read more about PixiJS Assets Management and Manifests in the official PixiJS documentation.

title: Overview
headings: Available components Point-axis props by component Why axis props? Property names Accessing the instance with Refs Using a pre-existing instance with the as prop Lifecycle note Omissions
text: Most of the PixiJS display components are available as Solid components in Pixi Solid. All components are named the same as their PixiJS counterparts and should be imported individually. This pattern also allows tree shaking, because each component imports only the parts of PixiJS that it needs. All of the components take the same props as their PixiJS counterparts, with the addition of event handlers. For the purpose, capabilities, and options of each component, see the PixiJS docs . These include: The names clash if you also import classes or types from directly. Alias the imports in that case: Or import all Pixi types under a namespace. Type-only imports are not bundled: All components support point-axis shorthand props for fine-grained reactivity. The specific axes available depend on the component type: SolidJS tracks changes by reference. Passing allocates a new object on every update, which both triggers the entire point to rebind and creates GC pressure. Axis props like and are plain values — no allocations, and only the changed axis triggers an update. All standard PixiJS properties available on a display object instance (e.g., x, y, rotation, alpha, width, height, scale, position, pivot, anchor, skew etc.) are directly available as props on the pixi-solid components. In addition to this, pixi-solid enhances these point-based properties (like position, scale, pivot, anchor, and skew) by providing individual axis props. This means you can control position.x independently using positionX, position.y with positionY, and similarly for scaleX, scaleY, pivotX, pivotY, anchorX, anchorY, skewX, and skewY. This allows for more granular control over these properties directly through JSX props without needing to create a new object for every update. As with SolidJS and the DOM, you can access the rendered object instance with a . In our case this is useful for calling methods on the PixiJS objects or interacting directly with PixiJS in an imperative way. We can use a variable or a callback function to access refs. Ref as a variable. Ref as a callback. All pixi-solid components accept an optional prop to use a pre-existing PixiJS instance instead of creating a new one. This is useful for sharing a single instance across parts of the tree, providing pre-configured instances, or injecting mock instances in tests. When is provided, pixi-solid assumes you own the instance's lifecycle and will not destroy it on unmount. You must destroy it manually when it is no longer needed. Some PixiJS classes are deliberately omitted, because wrapping them in a SolidJS component does not add much value: — Particles inside a are designed for maximum-performance, high-volume imperative updates. A dedicated SolidJS component for individual particles contradicts that goal. Create and manage particle instances imperatively with a as the parent. , , , , — These are low-level geometry classes used when building custom meshes. Create them imperatively with PixiJS and wrap in a custom component when needed. — May be added in the future; hasn't been evaluated enough to determine if a SolidJS component would be useful.

text: The component is the primary way to create a PixiJS application in a application. It handles creating and managing the HTML canvas element, the PixiJS Application instance, and provides context to child components for accessing the application and ticker. Automatically creates and manages a instance Wraps the canvas in a responsive container that automatically resizes Provides context for ticker-based utilities ( , , etc.) Accepts all standard PixiJS Application options as props Can be used standalone or with for more control Allows one per at a time; it can be unmounted and remounted The simplest way to use is standalone. title: Migrating to Solid 2
headings: Upgrade the packages Update the import paths Renamed and removed APIs Effects are split Async work and <Loading> Reactive writes are batched pixi-solid API changes Ref callbacks
text: 2 requires SolidJS 2. Component, hook, and utility names stay the same. Almost all of the work is in the SolidJS APIs around them. SolidJS publishes a complete migration guide . Read that for the full list. This page covers the parts that meet a pixi-solid project, and the changes to itself. Install SolidJS 2 and its web renderer, then add the compiler plugin: declares all three as peers. The supported range for and is . The compiler must use as the JSX renderer. See Project setup for the and Vite settings. no longer owns the JSX types or the store helpers. These are the ones that turn up in a pixi-solid scene. The SolidJS guide covers the rest. is removed with no replacement. and take a compute function and an effect function. The compute returns the value that the effect receives, and it is the only part that tracks. This is the pattern for binding a signal to a PixiJS class property: Async work is a computation that returns a Promise. Create it with and read it inside a boundary: A boundary covers its whole subtree and catches a pending read from any descendant. Place it around the smallest group that should wait. The is optional and replaces the children, so it sits wherever the boundary sits. Inside a Pixi tree the fallback must be a Pixi element, and a DOM element in that position throws . Put the boundary above the canvas to use a DOM fallback. See Asset loading and Asset manifests for the two loading patterns. A signal write does not change what a read returns until the batch flushes. Call before you assert: The testing helpers rely on this behavior. See Testing . accepts a , so an object or array replaces the removed prop. accepts a Solid . The callback form still works. A variable and an array of callbacks also typecheck now. The Solid compiler turns a variable into a callback that assigns to it, so the runtime only ever receives callbacks. returns a helper that applies the test providers. and accept an options object with an optional . calls its callback once. returns the value from that call. resets the Solid error halt in addition to unmounting. is available from the root exports. A ref callback is no longer a place for reactive work. In 1 it ran inside the component's owner, and it re-ran whenever a prop it read changed. It now runs without an owner, and it runs once. It has no owner. inside a ref callback never runs, an effect created inside one never disposes, and inside one throws, because a context read needs an owner. Move that work into in the component body, which runs after the ref has been assigned, and return a cleanup function: The receives a DOM element, and SolidJS clears the owner for DOM refs for the same reason, so the same rule applies there. It runs once. In 1 a ref callback re-ran whenever a prop it read changed, so a drawing command followed a signal. Use the prop instead: For any other component, move the read into a split effect: the compute function tracks the read, and the apply function calls into the instance. Reach for this when the value has no matching prop, such as 's , which is a getter with no setter. Passing it as a prop throws. Most PixiJS state does have a prop, and pixi-solid binds those props reactively. needs no effect at all. A read left inside a ref callback also reports in development.

title: useSmoothDamp
headings: Return Value Behavior Demo Code example
text: The function provides a reactive SolidJS signal that smoothly interpolates a numeric value towards a target value over time. The function returns an object with the following properties: - An accessor signal containing the current damped value - An accessor signal containing the current velocity - A function to set the current value directly, bypassing damping calculations for that frame. This allows you to "teleport" the value to a specific point. The velocity will continue to be calculated normally on the next frame. It internally manages the damping physics and keeps its updates synchronized with the PixiJS application's ticker, ensuring smooth animations that sync with your application's frame rate. This function is similar in functionality to Unity's which is based on Game Programming Gems 4, Chapter 1.10.
